newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-Pacific Link a thorn in First Pac's side.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Pacific Link a thorn in First Pac's side.

text.p: First Pacific Co Ltd says it is enjoying robust growth in its various businesses but its Hong Kong cellular telephone arm could see a decline of up to 40 percent in profits due to tough competition.
"Apart from the fly in the ointment which is called Pacific Link in Hong Kong, there is really nothing wrong with the group," managing director Manuel Pangilinan told Reuters late on Wednesday.
"We feel confident that we will show an increase in profit on a recurring basis," he said in an interview.
The Hong Kong conglomerate posted 32 percent growth in recurrent earnings in 1996 to HK$1.57 billion. Net profit fell 21 percent to HK$1.59 billion due to exceptional gains in 1995.

While Hong Kong-based telecommunications business Pacific Link Communications Ltd saw a rise of 38 percent in its 1996 profit contribution to HK$453 million, Pangilinan said fierce competition would lead to a sharp drop in 1997.
"I think the decline in earnings will be anywhere between 20 to 40 percent," he said, adding that the decline was likely to be nearer the higher end of the range.
The profit contribution from the whole telecoms business would suffer as a result although First Pacific's other telecommunications operations were doing well, Pangilinan said.
Telecommunications contributed about 27 percent to First Pacific's 1996 profit.

"I think it will be held back this year with the decline in earnings of Pacific Link," Pangilinan said. "We are tempering our own projections by the year 2000 but it will continue to be a major contributor to the earnings of the group."
First Pacific said the competitive environment would force it to restructure its Hong Kong telecommunications business.

"There is a range of possibilities -- get a strategic partner to help with the operating expertise, marketing expertise, financial capital or you attempt as well to consolidate the industry so there are fewer players," Pangilinan said.
He said First Pacific would welcome a strategic partner, "someone who is marketing oriented and an existing telco operator", for its Greater China telecoms operations.
The company's Asian telecommunications holding company, Asia Link, is currently talking to several parties and Pangilinan said any partnerships could result in exceptional gains.
But he declined to say who the company was in discussions with. "I can't be specific. These are big names."
First Pacific's other businesses are marketing and distribution which contributed 46 percent of 1996 profits, property which contributed 15 percent, and banking which contributed 12 percent.
"I think the rest are posting strong growth. Overall that is precisely the strength of the diversity," Pangilinan said.

He said First Pacific still planned to go ahead with a listing of its Philippine mobile phone operation Smart Communications in August or September despite a steep decline in the Philippine stock market.

But he said a flotation of First Pacific's other Philippine unit, Fort Bonifacio Development Corp, was unlikely to go ahead this year due to negative investor sentiment towards the Philippine real estate market.

"First Pacific has nothing to gain (from the Fort Bonifacio float) except for an exceptional profit which could arise from the flotation which we don't regard as a measure of performance of the group," Pangilinan said.

"If the Smart thing does happen, I would like to think that overall there will be very significant profit growth for the company. If we are successful in getting strategic partners for China then there will be more exceptional gains."
-- Hong Kong newsroom (852) 2843 6345
